title: Habakkuk: by faithfulness (Habakkuk 2:4)
hook: the Talmud says Habakkuk reduced the whole Torah to one line: the righteous live by faith (Makkot 24a)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Micah brought the peace of nations down to one person in the shade of a fig tree. Your line was none shall make them afraid. Who sat a little easier near you? Today, a prophet who opens with a complaint. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

"O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" That's how Habakkuk begins, in the King James. Not with a message for the people, but with the prophet arguing upward. He sees violence and strife, the law gone slack, the wicked hemming in the righteous, and he asks why God lets him watch it. An answer comes, and it troubles him even more, so he asks again. And then he does something stubborn. He climbs up to wait: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower." He's not coming down until he hears back.
screen: `HOW LONG SHALL I CRY?` → `THE ANSWER TROUBLES HIM MORE.` → `UP THE TOWER, TO WAIT.`

segments.voice: The answer, when it comes, starts with instructions about handwriting. "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it." Big letters, so even someone running past can read them. Then a warning about time: "though it tarry, wait for it." And then the line: "the just shall live by his faith." The Hebrew word under faith is emunah. In English, faith can sound like something in your head, a belief you hold about a thing. Emunah leans toward something you do with your whole life: steadiness, firmness, keeping faith. The same word turns up in Exodus, when Moses holds up his arms through a long battle and Aaron and Hur prop them up. The King James says his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. Steady: that's the Hebrew emunah. So the righteous live by steadiness. And notice the small word his. His faithfulness. Some readers hear the righteous person's own steadiness. Others hear God's faithfulness, the thing the righteous lean on while they wait. The Hebrew can carry both. Now the Talmud. In tractate Makkot, Rabbi Simlai teaches that Moses was given six hundred thirteen commandments, and that later voices gathered them into fewer and fewer lines. David set them on eleven, Isaiah on six, Micah, the prophet of the last two days, on three, Isaiah again on two. For the last step the rabbis weigh Amos, then settle on this: Habakkuk came and set them all on one. The righteous shall live by his faith. Not a rule about food or Shabbat, but the ground every rule stands on. One line, written large enough to read on the run.
screen: `WRITE IT PLAIN, TO READ ON THE RUN.` · `THOUGH IT TARRY, WAIT FOR IT.` · then, large: `THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY HIS FAITH.` · then: `EMUNAH: STEADY HANDS TILL SUNSET.` · then: `ALL OF IT, SET ON ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: For the practice, live today by one trust. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you're waiting on: an answer, a result, a person to change, a door to open. Notice how waiting feels in your body. Then, like Habakkuk on the tower, choose to stand where you are rather than run. Pick one steady thing you can trust today: a person who has kept their word, a habit that holds you, or, if you pray, God's faithfulness. Breathe as if your arms were being held up. You can let Habakkuk's words ride the breath: though it tarry, wait for it. The bell holds the time.
Habakkuk. The prophet who argued, climbed the tower to wait, and heard the line the Talmud says holds up all the rest: the just shall live by his faith. Today's word.
Your line: live by faithfulness. Today, keep one small promise exactly as you made it, on time, and let that be your steadiness. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews read Habakkuk among the Twelve, and the Talmud's tractate Makkot names Habakkuk 2:4 as the single line on which the commandments stand.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means believing something you can't prove.
what it means: emunah, steadiness. the righteous live by keeping faith while they wait.
what a scholar hears: the word for Moses' steady hands in Exodus, and the Talmud's claim that all the commandments stand on this one line.

notes: Audit pass: the Makkot 24a retelling had Habakkuk follow Micah directly ('and then'), skipping Isaiah's two and the Amos step that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak replaces with Habakkuk; now gives the sequence as the passage does (David 11, Isaiah 6, Micah 3, Isaiah 2, Amos weighed, Habakkuk 1) and names Rabbi Simlai. Day 827 no longer mentions this passage, so the two days no longer overlap. Path-wide KJV vs JPS 1917 question noted on day 827.

Makkot 24a paraphrased: Rabbi Simlai's 613 commandments, then Micah 'set them on three' and Habakkuk 'on one'. The number 613 is stated because the cited passage states it; please confirm the paraphrase.
Exodus 17:12: the Hebrew for 'steady' is emunah; confirm.
